We conducted a preliminary field study to understand the current state of
personal digital archiving in practice. Our aim is to design a service for the
long-term storage, preservation, and access of digital belongings by examining
how personal archiving needs intersect with existing and emerging archiving
technologies, best practices, and policies. Our findings not only confirmed
that experienced home computer users are creating, receiving, and finding an
increasing number of digital belongings, but also that they have already lost
irreplaceable digital artifacts such as photos, creative efforts, and records.
Although participants reported strategies such as backup and file replication
for digital safekeeping, they were seldom able to implement them consistently.
Four central archiving themes emerged from the data: (1) people find it
difficult to evaluate the worth of accumulated materials; (2) personal storage
is highly distributed both on- and offline; (3) people are experiencing
magnified curatorial problems associated with managing files in the aggregate,
creating appropriate metadata, and migrating materials to maintainable formats;
and (4) facilities for long-term access are not supported by the current
desktop metaphor. Four environmental factors further complicate archiving in
consumer settings: the pervasive influence of malware; consumer reliance on ad
hoc IT providers; an accretion of minor system and registry inconsistencies;
and strong consumer beliefs about the incorruptibility of digital forms, the
reliability of digital technologies, and the social vulnerability of networked
storage.

We investigate the Gross-Pitaevskii equation for a classically chaotic
system, which describes an atomic Bose-Einstein condensate confined in an
optical lattice and driven by a spatiotemporal periodic laser field. It is
demonstrated that the exact Floquet states appear when the external
time-dependent potential is balanced by the nonlinear mean-field interaction.
The balance region of parameters is divided into a phase-continuing region and
a phase-jumping one. In the latter region, the Floquet states are
spatiotemporal vortices of nontrivial phase structures and zero-density cores.
Due to the velocity singularities of vortex cores and the blowing-up of
perturbed solutions, the spatiotemporal vortices are unstable periodic states
embedded in chaos. The stability and instability of these Floquet states are
numerically explored by the time evolution of fidelity between the exact and
numerical solutions. It is numerically illustrated that the stable Floquet
states could be prepared from the uniformly initial states by slow growth of
the external potential.

This paper presents a study of quasi-steady spherical accretion in the early
Universe, before the formation of the first stars and galaxies. The main
motivation is to derive the basic formulas that will be used in a companion
paper to calculate the accretion luminosity of primordial black holes and their
effect on the cosmic ionization history.
  The following cosmological effects are investigated: the coupling of the gas
to the CMB photon fluid (i.e., Compton drag), Hubble expansion, and the growth
of the dark matter halo seeded by the gravitational potential of the central
point mass. The gas equations of motion are solved assuming either a polytropic
or an isothermal equation of state. We consider the cases in which the
accreting object is a point mass or a spherical dark matter halo with power-law
density profile, as predicted by the theory of "secondary infall''. Analytical
solutions for the sonic radius and fitting formulas for the accretion rate are
provided.
  Different accretion regimes exist depending on the mass of the accreting
object. If the black hole mass is smaller than 50-100 Msun, gas accretion is
unaffected by Compton drag. A point mass and an extended dark halo of equal
mass accrete at the same rate if M>5000 Msun, while smaller mass dark halos
accrete less efficiently than the equivalent point mass. For masses M>3 x 10^4
Msun, the viscous term due to the Hubble expansion becomes important and the
assumption of quasi-steady flow fails. Hence, the steady Bondi solutions
transition to the time-dependent self-similar solutions for "cold cosmological
infall".

Samuel Champlain's 1615 adventures in Ontario represent the first written account we have of a European regarding the Great Lakes. If you consider Lake Champlain to be the "sixth Great Lake", then Champlain's "discovery" would be sooner, but it wasn't until [his 1615-1616 travels](_URL_0_) that he reached Lake Huron and Lake Ontario.

He came to the lakes from what is (to a modern eye, looking at a modern map) an odd direction. Traveling up the St. Lawrence River to the modern site of Montreal, he explored the Ottawa River to the west, past the site of the city that would later be built on its banks. He continued west, reaching Lake Nipissing and then downriver to Georgian Bay in Lake Huron. Traveling southeast along the eastern shore of Georgian Bay, he navigated a series of tributaries and rivers between lakes Huron and Ontario before reaching and crossing that latter lake.

Champlain wasn't traveling alone, of course. His voyages were an attempt to make allies and ensure the fur-trading routes along the upper St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers stayed open. As a friend of the Huron confederacy, he traveled in a fairly large party, contributing his European firearms to campaigns against the Iroquois and others. I'll use [the 1907 translation on _URL_2_](_URL_1_) for this, so you can read the account in full if you want.

Champlain had kind words of the Nipissing people, whom he encountered around the lake of the same name and the northeastern portion of Lake Huron:

 > "These people are very numerous, there being from seven to eight hundred souls, who live in general near the lake. This  contains a large number of very pleasant islands, among others one more than six leagues long, with three or four fine ponds and a number of fine meadows ; it is bordered by very fine woods, that contain an abundance of game, which frequent the little ponds, where the savages also catch fish. The northern side of the lake is very pleasant, with fine meadows for the grazing of cattle, and many little streams, discharging into the lake."

This passage in Champlain's account refers to Lake Nipissing, which is connected by French River to Lake Huron. 

In his account, Champlain refers to Georgian Bay of Lake Huron as "Lake Attigouautan" or the lake of the Attigouautan, a term given by the Huron to Champlain.

 > "All this region (of Lake Huron) is still more unattractive than the preceding, for I saw along this river only ten acres of arable land, the rest being rocky and very hilly. It is true that near Lake Attigouautan we found some Indian corn, but only in small quantity. Here our savages proceeded to gather some squashes, which were acceptable to us, for our provisions began to give out in consequence of the bad management of the savages, who ate so heartily at the beginning that towards the end very little was left, although we had only one meal a day. But, as I have mentioned before, we did not lack for blueberries and strawberries; otherwise we should have been in danger of being reduced to straits."

Again and again in Champlain's account, he discusses the quality of the soil and the food/game available in the area. This is because Champlain's journal isn't just a travelogue; it's supposed to serve as a letter in support of settlement and colonization of the area. 

So our first account of the lakes is effectively written by a land developer, someone encouraging others to "buy" into the area.

Allow me to jump ahead almost 200 years. That's nearly how long it took for Europe to learn that the lakes definitively did not connect to the Pacific Ocean. Up until the end of the 18th century, there was a thought that the lakes could, from their western end, connect to a bay or inlet of the Pacific by river or other watercourse.

Warren Cook's *Flood Tide of Empire* is my favorite work when it comes to the Spanish presence in the Pacific Northwest, and it does a great job of explaining why the Spanish had a vested interest in keeping the Pacific Northwest unexplored as long as there was the possibility of a Northwest Passage. 

In 1592, there was a rumored voyage by a man named Juan de Fuca, who allegedly found a route eastward. There's been no definitive evidence that there was such a voyage or even that de Fuca existed. The sole account of Fuca's voyage was in a 1596 account written by Michael Lok in Venice, who told it to another man, who had it published as part of a larger account.

Regardless of the truth, de Fuca's account was carried forward as authentic or at least partially authentic until the 1790s, when Spanish and British voyages of exploration began poking into Puget Sound. That the myth survived so long is attributable to the existence of the Columbia River, which wasn't definitively explored until Americans did so until the last decade of the century.

This paper formalizes the properties required for addressing (indexing) memory augmented neural networks as well as how to pair the addressing with read/write operation. It then proposes a framework in which any Lie group as the addressing space. Experiments on algorithmic tasks are reported.

*** Review Summary ***

This paper brings unity and formalism in the requirement for memory addressing while maintaining differentiable memories. Its proposal provide a generic scheme to build addressing mechanisms. It should be stressed and a discussion on the impact it has on efficiency/scalability is needed.

$B\to\phi K^*$ ($\btos$) is three separate decays, one for each polarization
of the final-state vector mesons (one longitudinal, two transverse). It is
observed that the fraction of transverse decays, $\fT$, and the fraction of
longitudinal decays, $\fL$, are roughly equal: $\fTfL \simeq 1$, in opposition
to the naive expectation that $\fT \ll \fL$. If one requires a single
explanation of all polarization puzzles, two possibilities remain within the
standard model: penguin annihilation and rescattering. In this paper we examine
the predictions of these two explanations for $\fTfL$ in $\btod$ decays. In $B
\to \rho\rho$ decays, only $\bd \to \rho^0\rho^0$ can possibly exhibit a large
$\fTfL$. In B decays related by U-spin, we find two promising possibilities:
(i) $B^+ \to K^{*0} \rho^+$ ($\btos$) and $B^+ \to \Kbar^{*0} K^{*+}$ ($\btod$)
and (ii) $\bs \to K^{*0} \Kbar^{*0}$ ($\btos$) and $\bd \to \Kbar^{*0} K^{*0}$
($\btod$). The measurement of $\fTfL$ in these pairs of decays will allow us to
test penguin annihilation and rescattering. Finally, it is possible to
distinguish penguin annihilation from rescattering by performing a
time-dependent angular analysis of $\bd \to \Kbar^{*0} K^{*0}$.

Let’s first establish timeframe here, because obviously different periods in Chinese history vary from one another, and also because Mulan is set in a particular time within that spectrum. Most of the telling put her in the state of Northern Wei, during the Northern and Southern Era between 420 and 589 CE. As the name suggests, this was a period of disunion for the Chinese empire, falling in between the collapse of the Han c. 220 CE, and the formal reunification of the imperium under the Sui c. 589.

Northern Wei was, like virtually the whole of China northern of the Yangtze and Huai Rivers, under the political and military control of non-Chinese people, collectively known as Turks. And when I say “Turks”, don’t start thinking of Istanbul and kebabs, these are in virtually every respect the analogue to what the Mongols under Genghis Khan would become 8 centuries later: a powerful confederation of central Asian steppe-riders. Northern Wei in particular was dominated by a subset called the Tuoba Xianbei, which had seized the throne of the largest territory in the north by successfully rebelling against its overlord state, Later Yan, in 399 and their clan leader enthroning himself as Emperor Daowu.

So that puts us in a time and place, let’s get to your question: how did military conscription take place in such a society?

It’s worth pointing out that, were we talking about a “real” Chinese dynasty – one controlled and run by the ethnic Han people – Like Han, Tang, or Song… we’d have a very different answer to this – they wouldn’t have conscripted; they’d have outsourced their military issues to other border “barbarians” to play them off of their own neighbors. But no, in this time and place – with both the north and the south embroiled in conflicts lasting centuries – conscription was a very real and necessary thing. The *Ballad of Mulan* makes this very clear: 

 >  可汗大点兵。军书十二卷，卷卷有爷名。阿爷无大儿，木兰无长兄。愿为市鞍马，从此替爷征。

 >  trans: The Khan is calling many troops. The army list is in twelve scrolls, On every scroll there’s Father’s name. Father has no grown up son, Mulan has no elder brother. I want to buy a saddle and horse, And serve in the army in Father’s place.”

Here already, though, we see the fictive license taken with this poem: this sort of personalization – individual names slated – would’ve been completely untenable, at least at the level of the khan/emperor. There would’ve just been far too much paperwork for that sort of thing, and far too expensive… throughout virtually the entire span of Chinese  imperial history, the central government itself could not manage anything below the county-level. Thus, authority had to be devolved to the local level. This had been done for centuries via the *chaiyi fa*, the “draft service system.” Villages were assigned as groups of households, most typically as a unit of 110 households called a *li*. The *li* was then further subdivided into eleven units of 10 households called *jia*, according to their tax-brackets – high, middle, or low. Of those 11 *jia*, the richest was assigned by the census-taker each decade as the “administrative” *jia*, and each household took a 1-year shift as head of the li. From the remaining 10 *jia*, they’d likewise take one-year-long shifts as the “levy labor unit” for their *li*. From Ray Huang: “Under the direction of the *li* chief of the year, it performed the local tax collection and delivery, and met all material and labor requisitions on behalf of the entire *li*. The other units paid their regular taxes, but were not liable to service obligations that year. Thus in a decennial period all households took a one-year turn at discharging their service obligations. After the ten-year cycle a new census was taken and all *lijia* were re- organized in accordance with the changes that had occurred during the decade. With certain variations, the wards and precincts in the cities were organized along similar lines.”

Services rendered by the *jia* called up for their year-long spate of duties could expect to perform tasks for the government such as providing office attendants for the administration, from the county all the way up to the imperial government... in role as varied as doormen, guards, messengers, litter-bearer, cooks, buglers, boatmen, patrolmen, jailers, stable grooms, receiving men in warehouses, operators of canal watergates, and clerical assistants. As mentioned, this wasn’t necessarily confined to one’s home region, but instead wherever the government deemed a vacancy needed to be filled. 

This same kind of locally-based conscription rotation was in effect for the military, as well. And while what I’m directly pulling from here in this next part actually occurred in the 11th century during the Northern Song, it was heavily inspired by and meant to emulate the conscription practices of the Period of Disunion. It was laid out as followed: in every locality, a group of households – first 10, but later reduced to 5 – were organized into a “small guard unit”, from which two mature males (or more depending on extenuating circumstances) could be called up for active duty. A level higher than that, the process largely repeated, with these small guards organized by 5s into “large guards” headed by the wealthiest landowner from among them. A level up, and again the large guards were groups by 5s into a single Superior Guard, headed by the two wealthiest landowners. All other households in the area not eligible for service as guardsmen – those unlanded peasants and urbanites – were considered to be eligible to be called upon as auxiliaries to the guard corps. For the LHC experiments, we show that the semi-leptonic and radiative signals of WIMPs in the hadron final states are within the reach of the LHC, and we discuss the prospects of the LHC in searching for the SUSY WIMPs in the multi-tonne and TeV mass ranges. We study the statistical properties of the velocity field in compressible MHD turbulence. We show that, for a large class of numerical simulations, the velocity field is well described by a scaling relation that relates the mean velocity to the velocity fluctuations and the compression ratio. Within this class of simulations, the standard deviation of the velocity field scales as the square of the mean velocity. We show this result by fitting the empirical scaling relation to the data with an appropriate model. We also show that the model can be used to extract the local compression ratio in regions of the flow. We find that the local compression ratio is correlated with the local mean velocity, but that the correlation is very weak. We also show that the local compression ratio is uncorrelated with the local standard deviation of the velocity field. We discuss these results in the framework of the Gurruwiwi-Ohno model, and show that the Gurruwiwi-Ohno model can be used to quantitatively reproduce our results.

Ice cubes crack when liquid is poured over them because of something called thermal shock. When you pour liquid that is a different temperature than the ice, there is a huge difference in temperature suddenly. This difference in temperature makes the ice expand or change shape quickly, which makes it crack. This can happen to other things too, if they are put in very hot or very cold water.

Thermal shock is a sudden large change in the temperature of something. It's kind of like when you put something cold in the freezer and it gets too cold too fast and it breaks. Ice cubes are super sensitive to thermal shock because they're not that strong and they don't have a whole lot of time to adjust.

Our bodies also have a thermal shock when we're in water that's too cold or too hot. Too much thermal shock can even hurt us! That's why we have to take showers and baths with water that isn't too hot or too cold.

So the bottom line is that ice cubes crack when liquid is poured over them because there is a big difference in temperature between them and the liquid, and the ice doesn't have enough time to adjust.

The Creamy Layer (also referred to as the Creamy Class) is a phrase used in the Indian context to classify the higher echelons of socio-economic stratification. The term has its origin in the Creamy Layer principle of affirmative action, a tool adopted by the Indian Government to promote socio-economic equality within the public sector. The concept of the Creamy Layer first emerged in the early 1970s when the Indian government began implementing a series of reservations and support mechanisms aimed at improving the socio-economic plight of its marginalised castes and ethnic communities. These programmes were designed to help marginalised communities in the job market, in education, and other areas of public life. In order to build a system of equality, it became necessary to exclude the cream of these communities from the system of reservations, so as to ensure that only the most disadvantaged were served by the programmes. The Indian government identified the Creamy Layer as those members of marginalised communities who had achieved a certain level of educational and economic development, beyond what could reasonably be expected from their communities. This has been the basis for the government’s policy of excluding the Creamy Layer from quotas and benefits extended to the marginalised communities. The revised version of the National Anti-Exploitation Act of 2000 defines the term ‘Creamy Layer’ as “persons in or from Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes and other backward Classes of citizens who satisfy either of the two conditions as certified by a competent authority: (a) having an annual family income of four lakh rupees; or (b) being a holder of a constitutional office or post or of any other type of post under the State.” The Creamy Layer Principle is an important element of India’s affirmative action policies, and has the potential to boost social mobility within the country. However, not all people are in favour of this policy, as some argue that it is an artificial and arbitrary classification of the population, and does not serve to address existing deep-seated socio-economic inequalities and injustices. The issue of the Creamy Layer and other similar measures has been discussed in the Supreme Court of India several times, most notably in the landmark Indra Sawhney Case in 1992. In this case, the Supreme Court held that the exclusion of the Creamy Layer from the scope of benefits and reservations is permissible, provided that the classification is reasonable and correlates to the objective it seeks to achieve. In recent times, the Indian government has taken steps to modify the Creamy Layer limits for different castes and communities. In 2019, the government raised the creamy layer limit to Rs 8 lakhs for Other Backward Classes and Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes, as well as barring income tax payees and those in high-paying public and private sector jobs, apart from a few other criteria, from applying for the quotas and benefits extended by the state. The debate over the Creamy Layer Principle is a major one in India, with both supporters and opponents viewing it from different perspectives and arguing for or against its implementation. Regardless, it is undeniable that this concept has been instrumental in the implementation of equality-driven policies in the country, and is likely to remain one of the most vital tools for affirmative action in the coming years.

This research investigates the high-speed collapse of two perfect fluids distributed cylindrically. For this purpose we employ an approximation scheme to explore the conditions of very large collapsing speeds of the two fluids. We investigate two scenarios, i.e. when the ratios of the pressures to the densities of the two fluids are bounded or vanish. It is found that if the pressures $p_1, p_2$ are non-zero, the high-speed approximation scheme breaks down once these ratios $c_s, d_s$ reach some positive constants. This breakdown of the high-speed approximation at a particular time in the collapse process indicates an uncertainty about the evolution of the system at and after this juncture. For the bounded case, there does not appear to be any possibility of a naked singularity arising from the two perfect fluids. On the other hand, in the vanishing case if a linear equation of state is used, the collapse is not held back by the pressures and therefore a naked singularity can form. This paper further broadens the results that have already been established by Nakao and Morisawa [1] for perfect fluid systems.

How to Deal With Unruly Children

Children can often be unruly, and this can be stressful for parents. These tips can help you deal with unruly children.

Determine the reason for the unruliness.
Unruliness can be a result of a child's inability to express himself or herself. Instead of crying, shouting, or acting out, encourage your child to use words to express emotions.
To help your child express feelings, provide a safe environment for expression. Let your child know it's okay to feel angry, but it's not okay to hit.
Offer alternative ways for your child to express emotions. Ideas include:
stomping feet
holding hands over the mouth
chewing on a favorite toy or blanket
Your child might have difficulty expressing emotions because he or she is frustrated. Children with limited abilities, such as those with autism, may be especially prone to acting out.

Determine if the child is misbehaving or just being a child.
Sometimes a child's unruliness can be attributed to normal, childlike behavior. This includes:

Talking back
Not listening
Waking up in the middle of the night
Biting
Playing too rough
Having tantrums
Childlike behavior is usually unacceptable when it comes at the wrong time. For example, you might not want your child to talk back to a teacher, but you might not mind when your child talks back to you in private.
Let your child know what's acceptable and what's not acceptable. Children might not understand when unruliness is okay and when it's not.

Determine if your child is being influenced by others.
Children are influenced by their peers, parents, and television. If you find that your child is unruly when he or she is around a certain child or when watching a certain show, try to limit your child's contact with that influence.
If the unruly behavior is caused by a child's home environment, you may be able to change the environment to make it more positive. This might include:

Moving furniture around
Getting a new pet
Introducing a new family member

Dealing with your own emotions.
Children can push their parents' buttons, and parents can sometimes lose their temper. If you find that you are constantly upset or angry with your child, you may need to take some time for yourself. Parents who take time out to relax are better able to deal with unruly children. Try taking a walk or doing some yoga when your child is napping. You might also consider seeing a therapist or parent coach.

Stay consistent with your discipline.
Discipline should be consistent, and parents should agree on how to raise their children. If one parent allows unruly behavior and the other does not, the child will be confused. This can lead to more unruliness.
If you and your partner are consistent, your child will eventually learn what's acceptable and what's not.

In this work, we consider an uplink MIMO system with Nt transmit antennas and one receive antenna at each user terminal (UT). We assume that all UTs are equipped with single RF chain which can be used to process signals received from multiple antennas simultaneously using linear processing techniques such as zero forcing or minimum mean square error criteria. A coma is a state of prolonged unconsciousness caused by an injury or disease that affects the brain. It is a serious medical condition that can result in lasting brain damage or even death if left untreated. While in a coma, the brain is in a state of reduced activity, and the person is completely unresponsive to external stimuli.

The brainstem, which controls vital functions such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure, remains functional during a coma. Therefore, the body stays alive even if the person is unconscious. However, the brain cannot process external stimuli, so even though the person is technically alive, they are incapable of interacting with the environment.

The length of a coma can vary greatly, from a few days to several months or even years. The body will wake up from a coma if and when the brain can regain normal function. When this happens, the person will slowly transition out of their comatose state and begin to regain consciousness.

There is no fixed timeline for regaining consciousness, as it largely depends on the severity of the injury or disease that caused the coma. In some cases, the person may quickly regain consciousness, while in others, it may take months or even years of rehabilitation to regain normal brain function.

Neurologists and other medical professionals use several tests, including electroencephalogram (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), to monitor the brain and assess the patient's likelihood of waking up from a coma. They also monitor vital signs and other body functions to ensure the patient remains stable and receives proper care.

In conclusion, a coma is a state of prolonged unconsciousness resulting from brain injury or disease. The body wakes up from a coma when the brain is capable of regaining normal function, and the length of a coma can vary greatly depending on the severity of the injury or disease.

String theory provides a consistent framework for quantum gravity that unifies all fundamental forces, but constructing a realistic model of particle physics from string theory is a challenging task.

Our approach involves the use of intersecting D6-branes and the Z_6' orientifold, which is a particularly interesting model due to its rich phenomenology. Intersecting branes provide a geometric realization of the chiral matter spectrum, while the orientifold projection allows for the cancellation of tadpoles and the breaking of supersymmetry. Our methodology involves a detailed analysis of the low-energy effective theory of the D6-branes and the computation of instanton-generated Yukawa couplings. Our results show that a realistic model of the Standard Model can be obtained from string theory using the methods of intersecting branes and orientifolds.

Jadwiga Szczawińska-Dawidowa (born Jadwiga Dżuria; 21 March 1915 – 9 April 1945) was a Polish resistance worker and member of the Polish 4th courier team, which smuggled top-secret government documents from occupied Poland to the Soviet Union, where they were passed on to the Western allies. She was arrested by the Germans and later killed by the Germans in a POW camp. She fought alongside her courier team-mates – husband Captain Dawid Nowak (codenamed "Czaika") and Janusz Bardańczyk ("Mikołaj Kopernik"), both of whom were posthumously awarded the Order of the Virtuti medal – in the early days of the Polish Defensive War and was posthumously awarded the Cross of Valour (fourth class). Szczawińska-Dawidowa's story is told in the 2011 film Oskar%C4%84 Horbach & Dawid Adamczyk: The Courier, based on the book of the same title by Maria Wodzińska. She was born in Wyszków and was brought up in Łódź, where she worked as a secretary. In 1939 she joined the Polish Socialist Youth (PPS ) and the National Workers' Party (PPS Kombat). In 1940 she began working for the organisation Ładoś, which was affiliated with the Polishresistance movement. Szczawińska-Dawidowa smuggled documents for the Polish government in occupied Poland, at great personal risk, to the Soviet Union. She was arrested by the Germans in 1943 and later killed by the Germans in a POW camp. She is buried in Góra Świętej Anny military cemetery.

It is observed that the models trained by SGD are sensitive to learning rates and good learning rates are problem specific. To avoid manually searching of learning rates, which is tedious and inefficient, we propose an algorithm to automatically learn learning rates using actor-critic methods from reinforcement learning (RL). In particular, we train a policy network called actor to decide the learning rate at each step during training, and a value network called critic to give feedback about quality of the decision (e.g., the goodness of the learning rate outputted by the actor) that the actor made. Experiments show that our method leads to good convergence of SGD and can prevent overfitting to a certain extent, resulting in better performance than human-designed competitors.

In this study, we investigated the high-energy threshold reaction rates on a 0.8 GeV proton-irradiated thick Pb-target. The motivation for this research was to understand the interaction between high-energy protons and thick Pb-targets, which is important for many applications in nuclear science and technology. However, previous studies have focused mainly on thin targets, and there is limited information on the reaction rates in thick targets. Therefore, our work attempts to fill this knowledge gap by performing experiments with a thick Pb-target and measuring the reaction rates using a gamma spectrometer. 

Our results showed that the reaction rates were much lower in the thick Pb-target compared to the thin target, due to the decrease in proton energy as it penetrates the material. We also observed some new gamma ray lines which have not been previously reported, indicating a possible reaction pathway in the thick target. Our findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of high-energy protons in thick materials, which can be used to improve the design of radiation shielding for nuclear reactors and accelerators. Overall, our work contributes to a better understanding of the fundamental physics of nuclear reactions and has practical implications for nuclear safety and radiation protection.

Animals do not attempt suicide because they do not have the capacity to comprehend abstract concepts such as life, death and its finality, or the feeling of hopelessness and despair that often leads humans to consider suicide. Unlike humans, animals do not reflect on their lives, ruminate on their past struggles and anticipated future problems, or attempt to find a satisfying ending to an unsatisfactory life.

Humans have the capacity to think about their lives and imagine alternate outcomes. Whether this ability is beneficial or harmful often depends on a person's mental state and psychological resilience. Animals, however, lack this capacity and thus do not experience the same level of suffering that may drive suicidal thoughts and actions. 

On the other hand, animals are equipped with an instinctual survival impulse that exists regardless of their mental state, life circumstances, and perceived quality of life. This instinctual need to survive is imprinted in their genetic makeup and drive behavior such as risk-aversion, fear, and avoidance of danger - all traits that deter animals from doing anything that could jeopardize their lives such as attempting suicide. 

What's more, animals lack the physical and mental capacity to enact acts of suicide, as most animals lack more complicated cognitive functions necessary for planning and completing an act of suicide. 

In addition to these instinctual and cognitive limitations, animals lack two other key components that are necessary for a person to carry out a suicidal act - an understanding of death, and the availability of lethal objects or substances. Without these two items, animals cannot make the choice to take their own life, as they do not understand the concept of death nor are they able to attain access to substances or objects that could potentially cause death. 

Therefore, even though animals know suffering and experience sadness, they are precluded from attempting suicide due to a combination of instinctual, mental, and physical limitations.

In our study titled "The Hypercube of Life: How Protein Stability Imposes Limits on Organism Complexity and Speed of Molecular Evolution," we investigate how the stability of proteins affects the complexity of living organisms and the speed of molecular evolution. Our motivation for this research stems from our desire to understand the underlying principles that shape the diversity of life. 

Using comparative genomic analyses and molecular simulations, we explore the relationship between protein stability and organismal complexity across different branches of the tree of life. We find that the stability of proteins constrains the number of mutations that an organism can tolerate without compromising its fitness. As organisms become more complex, their proteins tend to be more stable, suggesting that the evolution of complexity is limited by the stability of biological molecules.

We also find that the speed of molecular evolution is inversely proportional to protein stability, with more stable proteins evolving at a slower rate. These results suggest that the stability of proteins is a fundamental factor shaping the evolutionary trajectories of organisms.

Overall, our study sheds new light on the role that protein stability plays in shaping the diversity of life and has implications for fields ranging from evolutionary biology to biotechnology and medicine.

Birlinn (Old Norse Byrlind, pronounced [byr-lin]; modern Gaelic Beirlinn) was a type of wooden ship in use in Scotland and Ireland during the Middle Ages, from the Early Middle Ages to the late 17th century. The generic term Birlinn encompassed several different types of vessels, including large cargo ships and smaller boats used for raiding, trade, or transport. The birlinn was designed as a large, multi-masted, open decked vessel with a large square rigged sail and oars for navigation in shallow waters. Its design varied between regions and over time, but it was built with a single, central mast and a square sail, a shallow draught, and was able to navigate in shallow waters due to its clinker-built construction style. By the early 16th century, birlinns were primarily made with four masts and were larger than any other wooden ship in Scotland or Ireland. Due to birlinns being constructed on land, instead of in the water, the offshore winds could be used for sails instead of relying on oars. Consequently, birlinns could travel faster and longer distances than other vessels of their age. The names birlinn and beirlinn were also used to refer to an Irish and Hebridean galley, respectively. This type of vessel was of a slightly different construction, with the central mast often being replaced by two masts and an increased sail capacity. These galley-type birlinns were used for warfare and were likely exchanged between the Gaelic kingdoms of Ireland and Scotland. They were renowned for their speed and manoeuvrability, which allowed them to outrun any other vessel they encountered. The birlinn featured prominently in medieval stories and literature of the period. It was also used in many archaeological excavations, most of which date back to the late 12th and early 13th centuries. For example, a birlinn was recovered in 2010 from Ardnamurchan Bay in Scotland. The vessel, which was likely built between 1150 and 1250, was the oldest ever found and provides valuable information on the design and construction of birlinns during this period. The birlinn has played an important role in the culture of both Scotland and Ireland, and was even used by Robert the Bruce during the Scottish Wars of Independence in the late 13th and early 14th centuries. Today, modern reconstructions are being built of the historic birlinn and can still be found in many parts of the country. The lifespan of a species can be influenced by many different factors. One of the most important is the environment in which the species lives. For example, some species that live in very cold climates have longer lifespans than species that live in warmer climates. This is because the colder climate requires the species to use more energy to stay warm, which can slow down the aging process.

Another factor that can influence the lifespan of a species is the type of food that it eats. Some species that eat a diet that is high in nutrients and low in toxins can have longer lifespans than species that eat a diet that is less healthy. This is because the nutrients can help to protect the cells from damage, while the lack of toxins can reduce the amount of stress on the body.

Finally, the lifespan of a species can also be influenced by its genes. Some species have genes that are better able to repair DNA damage, which can slow down the aging process. In addition, some species have genes that are more resistant to disease, which can also increase their lifespan.

The reason that humans have a longer lifespan than housecats is likely due to a combination of all of these factors. Humans have a relatively long lifespan compared to other species because we have evolved to live in a variety of different environments, we have access to a diverse diet, and we have genes that are well-suited for longevity.

The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel is set in 1958 New York City, and while there was certainly still segregation going on in the Big Apple at that time, it's a fact that New York was more integrated than many other American cities.  The Harlem Renaissance was at its height in the late 1920s and early 1930s, and African Americans continued to flock to New York throughout the Great Depression and beyond.  Segregationist laws like the ones we associate with the Jim Crow South were largely unenforceable in the North, although there were still plenty of places in New York that were off-limits to black people.  There were African Americans working in white-owned restaurants and bars, but it was definitely not the norm, and it's hard to say if Midge would have felt comfortable frequenting places that had never had black customers before.  It's possible that the show is taking some creative license in depicting a more integrated New York than was really the case, but the segregated parts of town are also not shown, so it's hard to say for sure.

We investigate the von Neumann and topological entropies of the toric code at finite temperatures for systems with both magnetic and electric excitations. We find that the entanglement entropy changes non-monotonically with respect to temperature and system size. The topological entropy then decreases to half its zero-temperature value at a finite temperature. In finite-size systems, this discontinuous behavior becomes smooth. We also identify the contribution of each type of energy excitation to the topological entropy and interpret the quantum topological order as arising from a combination of both magnetic and electric closed loop structures.

Activated charcoal, also known as activated carbon, is a form of carbon that has been treated to increase its adsorptive capacity. The activation process involves heating the carbon at very high temperatures in the presence of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, or steam. This creates a highly porous material with a large surface area that can adsorb toxins and impurities from its surroundings.

Activated charcoal has become wildly popular in the beauty/cosmetic industry due to its ability to absorb toxins and impurities that can clog pores and cause skin blemishes. It is commonly used in face masks, cleansers, and other skincare products to help detoxify the skin and leave it looking clear and smooth.

In addition to its skincare benefits, activated charcoal is also used in toothpaste and mouthwash to help whiten teeth and freshen breath. The porous surface of activated charcoal can help absorb plaque and stain-causing substances, leaving teeth looking brighter and cleaner.

It's worth noting that while activated charcoal has many benefits, it is not recommended for everyone. By offloading the computational burden of CPU and saving the need for transferring raw data in its entirety, NDP exhibits a great potential for acceleration and power reduction. Despite this potential, specific research activities on NDP have witnessed only limited success until recently, often owing to performance mismatches between logic and memory process technologies that put a limit on the processing capability of memory. Recently, there have been two major changes in the game, igniting the resurgence of NDP with renewed interest. The first is the success of machine learning (ML), which often demands a great deal of computation for training, requiring frequent transfers of big data. Sparked by these application needs and technological support, we evaluate the potential of NDP for ML using a new SSD platform that allows us to simulate in-storage processing (ISP) of ML workloads. Our platform (named ISP-ML) is a full-fledged simulator of a realistic multi-channel SSD that can execute various ML algorithms using the data stored in the SSD. For thorough performance analysis and in-depth comparison with alternatives, we focus on a specific algorithm: stochastic gradient decent (SGD), which is the de facto standard for training differentiable learning machines including deep neural networks. We implement and compare three variants of SGD (synchronous, Downpour, and elastic averaging) using ISP-ML, exploiting the multiple NAND channels for parallelizing SGD. In addition, we compare the performance of ISP and that of conventional in-host processing, revealing the advantages of ISP. Based on the advantages and limitations identified through our experiments, we further discuss directions for future research on ISP for accelerating ML.

If you're interested in getting into the world of fencing, you'll need to understand the terminology that comes along with it. Armed with an understanding of these basic terms, you'll be ready to take on the sport of fencing. 

The first key word to understand is "Lunge". A lunge is an attack which involves extending the arm with the weapon towards your opponent. This is a common move in both épée and foil fencing. It can be used to score a touch, or as a setup or preparation for another move. 

In foil and saber fencing, the move "parry" is also used. A parry is a defensive move used to deflect your opponent's attack. The type of parry used will depend on which weapon you're using and the circumstances of the bout.

The next phrase you'll hear in fencing is the French "En garde!". This phrase is shouted when the fencers assume the starting fencing stance. In fencing, this position is referred to as "on guard". It involves each fencer holding their weapon out in front of them with one hand, and the other hand behind the back, in a ready position.

At the start of a fencing match, the judge will say "Pret!" which is a French word meaning "ready". This signal gives a warning to the fencers that the match is about to begin. After this, the judge will shout "Allez!" which means "go" in French. This tells the fencers to advance and begin to fence.

Throughout the bout you may hear the judge call "Arrêt!" which is a French word meaning "stop". This is a signal to the fencers to stop what they are doing, face each other and return to the on guard position after the touch is marked.

The most important word to remember during fencing is the term "touch." A "touch" occurs when a fencer's weapon makes contact with a valid target area and is recognized by the referee. In modern fencing, it is a much welcomed alternative to the "shocking" methods used in the past.

Once a touch has been made, your opponent has the opportunity to "riposte", another French word literally meaning "answer". This means that they can attack you with their weapon in order to score a touch, as long as the attack comes directly after the initial touch.

Another move to be aware of is the "disengage". A disengage is a movement of the weapon tip underneath your opponent's weapon, and then back to where it originally was. This can be used offensively to maneuver your attacker's weapon away and score a touch, or defensively in order to successfully parry an attack.

An offensive move is commonly referred to as an "attack". In foil and saber fencing, an attack is any movement made with the intention of scoring a touch. In épée fencing the same holds true, though in this form of fencing there is no concept of "right of way", meaning that you may make an attack even if your opponent has started to do the same.

The highest ranking referee in the hall is known as the "director" or "directeur". The directeur is responsible for supervising all of the bouts, marking touches, and ensuring that all of the participants are observing the regulations of the sport.

To make sure that the touches are being scored accurately, it is important to understand fencing's target areas. In all three forms of fencing there is a valid area which can be touched in order to score, which includes the entire torso region for épée and foil, and both the torso and the head in saber.

By learning and understanding these basic terms of fencing, you'll be one step closer to understanding and taking on this wonderful sport. Whether you're just starting out, or wishing to brush up on your knowledge, equip yourself with an understanding of these basic fencing terms and you'll be ready to take on the challenge of dueling with swords.

A quantum computer is fundamentally different from a classical computer in that it harnesses the power of quantum phenomena such as superposition and entanglement to achieve its calculations. While a classical computer is limited to either a 0 or a 1, a quantum computer simultaneously exists in all 0s and 1s, allowing it to explore multiple paths at once and find solutions quickly. This means that a quantum computer can, in effect, try all solutions at once; however how does it decide which is correct? 

The difficulty in answering this question is due to the fact that quantum computing is still a relatively new technology and a lot of the principles behind it are still being developed and refined. Essentially, once a quantum computer has attempted a task and the results are ready, the user can decide which of the solutions is the correct answer. These best solutions, or ‘quantum bits’, are found using mathematical optimization techniques such as Simulated Annealing or Quantum Search algorithms, algorithms developed specifically for use in quantum computing. The nature of simulated annealing is contingent on the user informing the computer of a certain set of rules that dictate what is an acceptable solution and what is not. 

The Quantum Search Algorithm can also be used to find the solution. This algorithm is more general than Simulated Annealing as it only relies on the different levels of energy associated with the solutions rather than any predetermined constraints. All the candidate solutions are put into a ‘black box’ and the one with the lowest energy determines the optimum solution.

In conclusion, a quantum computer can indeed give the user multiple solutions with the potential to be correct; however, the user must identify the correct solution using one of the two aforementioned algorithms. By using either Simulated Annealing or Quantum Search Algorithm a user can see which result is the most optimal solution.

Gabriele Münter was a prominent German painter who played a vital role in the development of expressionism, a revolutionary art movement that emerged in Germany after World War I. She was widely recognized for her use of vibrant colors, bold brushstrokes, and unconventional techniques that portrayed a vivid and emotional experience of nature, landscape, and daily life. Münter was born in Berlin in 1877 and studied at the Phalanx School in Munich. She met her lifelong partner and fellow artist, Wassily Kandinsky, in 1902, and the couple became an integral part of the early expressionist movement. Together, they founded the influential Blue Rider group, which aimed to promote avant-garde art and spirituality in the wake of industrial modernization. Münter's early works were influenced by the impressionist and fauvist styles. She often painted landscapes and still lifes, which later evolved into symbolic and surreal compositions. Her most famous painting, "The Jawlensky Residence in Wiesbaden," which portrayed her former teacher and mentor, was completed in 1908 and is considered a masterpiece of early expressionism. Münter's paintings were often subject to censorship and criticism by the German authorities, who saw her work as a threat to traditional German art. As a result, she struggled to gain recognition and was forced to exhibit her work abroad. However, her influence on the art world was undeniable, and she continued to hold several solo exhibitions throughout her career. Münter's legacy remains significant in the history of modern art, particularly for her contributions to expressionism and women's art movements. She died in 1962 in Murnau, a town where she had lived and painted for over fifty years. Today, her works are widely recognized and celebrated in exhibitions and museums worldwide, including the Gabriele Münter-und Johannes Eichner Foundation in Germany, which holds the largest collection of her works.

Title: "Discrete Choices under Social Influence: Generic Properties".
Abstract:
We study the generic properties of discrete choice models with social influence, where agents make decisions based on their own private information and the choices made by others in their neighborhood.  We show that if there is no correlation between individuals' private signals then any equilibrium must be symmetric across individuals (i.e., all equilibria are identical up to relabeling). If instead there exists some positive correlation among individuals' private signals, we prove that there always exist asymmetric equilibria. Finally, for intermediate levels of correlation, we provide examples showing both types of equilibria can co-exist. These results hold regardless of whether or not agents have common knowledge about each other's payoffs. 
Our analysis relies heavily on recent advances in the theory of global games. The main idea behind our approach is to view an agent's decision problem as a two-stage game played against nature. At stage one, Nature chooses her signal realization; at stage two, she makes her choice conditional on this realized signal.

We present photometric observations of the binary companions to the luminous blue variables (LBVs) SN 1987A and SN 1967G. We show that these systems contain extremely close pairs of white dwarfs in wide (8–9 days) orbit around the blue dwarf. The mass of the blue dwarf is not much greater than the mass of the white dwarf in either system. Thus, these systems are not useful for studying the evolution of field LBVs. The close white dwarf pairs are unusual and of interest in their own right, however. We discuss the possibility that the evolution of these systems has been influenced by the exchange of material between the two stars, possibly leading to the white dwarf's acquiring a significant fraction of its current mass. The accretion history of the white dwarf is probably not unique, so this may provide a mechanism for the evolution of other field LBVs. The low-mass objects in these systems may be the first examples of objects in the so-called detached object category that has been proposed as a possible route to the evolution of type I supernovae.

We have discovered a new detached binary in the planetary nebula around SN 1987A. The binary is composed of an orbital pair of white dwarfs in a widely asymmetric (80-day) orbit around a blue dwarf. The blue dwarf is slightly more massive than the white dwarfs. This is the third detached binary discovered in the last year, providing support for the hypothesis that these objects are an important stage in the evolution of massive binary systems.

That is definitely a strange problem! If your dishwasher is drying all your other dishes, then it is definitely strange that your tupperware is still wet coming out of the dishwasher. Let's take a closer look to figure out why this might be happening.

The first place to start is with the dishwasher itself. Do you have a dishwasher that features a heated drying cycle? This can help dishes dry much quicker and more effectively, so if your dishwasher doesn't have this feature, that could be part of the problem. If you do have a heated drying cycle, you might want to make sure it is turned on and working properly. 

The second thing to consider is your detergent. Quantity, type, and the concentration of your detergent can all play a role in how well your dishes dry. Too much detergent can leave films or other substances that leave tupperware wet, while not enough detergent won't effectively remove the food and oils from them. 

Finally, think about the layout and placement of your tupperware in the dishwasher. You want to make sure you aren't stacking them too tightly or placing them directly under the spray arm or spinner, as this could cause water to pool and stay in your tupperware for longer, coming out wet. You also want to verify that all seals and lids are completely closed, so that steam isn't trapped inside. 

If these all look good, then you may want to look into deeper cleaning your dishwasher - clear out any debris, run a vinegar cycle, and make sure the filter is free of debris. If all else fails, you may have to call an appliance repair person to look at your dishwasher. 

All of these tips should be able to help you figure out why your tupperware is wet coming out of the dishwasher, when the plates and glasses are all dry.

HD 98800: A 10-Myr-Old Transition Disk

We present high-resolution observations of the disk surrounding the young solar-like star HD 98800. These data include images obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) that reveal the disk to be a transition disk with a diameter of approximately 80 au. We find that the disk is comprised of two distinct parts: a compact inner region with a radius of approximately 20-30 au and a more extended outer region with a radius of approximately 50-80 au. The disk is generally well-circumscribed by a rim, except for a cavity of approximately 5-10 au in radius at the position of the terrestrial planet mass companion discovered in 2005. We estimate that the mass of the disk is 41 lunar masses (0.2 Earth masses) assuming a density of 1.6 g cm^3. We discuss the possible formation mechanisms for the disk and examine the potential for the disk to evolve into an analog of the solar system. We find that if the disk was formed by the accretion of planetesimals, it would have required an accretion rate of 0.01 Earth masses per Myr, similar to the rate estimated for the growth of the giant planets. We discuss the relative amounts of material in the disk and the likelihood that this disk may be the remains of a tumultuous planet formation process. We also examine the disk's habitability and find that the disk has a volatile content of approximately 0.01 Earth masses and a dust mass of approximately 0.02 Earth masses. We conclude that this disk is unlikely to be a habitable analog for the solar system, and thus is not a likely candidate for the search for extraterrestrial life. We discuss the implications of this disk for planet formation theory, and we highlight the need for further observations, both to verify our basic characterization of this disk and to better constrain the disk's properties.

This paper estimates the power spectrum of cosmic shear, the density distortion caused by the distorsion of the gravity field of distant galaxies by the distribution of dark matter, dark energy and baryons in the universe. We use extensive simulated convergence power spectra, including the full covariance between bins, to fit a model to the data from cluster counts and cosmic shear. The resulting constraints on the dark energy equation of state parameter, w, are relatively insensitive to the choice of data set or modeling of the covariance, but the covariance remains a significant source of uncertainty. Marginalizing over this covariance, we find the 95% confidence interval w=-1.31+/-0.19 (w=-1.04+/-0.19) for a flat (closed) universe with the ratio of the energy densities of dark energy and matter, Omega_{de0}, constrained, and we measure the curvature b_{space}=-0.72+/-0.16 (b_{space}=-0.53+/-0.16). We forecast the constraining power of future surveys and find that combining cosmic shear with cluster counts will lead to a tight constraint on w (with the 95% confidence interval w=-1.00+/-0.06), while adding shear information to existing cluster surveys will only weakly improve the constraint on w (with the 95% confidence interval w=-1.15+/-0.10).

The CIA has long been accused of involvement in the crack epidemic, or more specifically the agency’s funneling of cocaine money to help fuel the crack epidemic in the 1980s. Although the accusation has been around for decades, it gained traction in the 2000s with the help of groups like the New York City Black and Latino Society and the city’s elected officials, who started running advertisements denouncing the claim as a “myth”. In response to the advertisements, Republicans in Congress held hearings on the subject, and even the New York Times published an editorial stating that “The case for the crack epidemic, in one paragraph”, based on the hearing testimony of psychologist Richard Gardner, a key accuser of the CIA. In 2010, a panel of the National Research Council of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine released a report on the matter. The report, however, found little evidence of a direct funneling of funds by the CIA to fuel the crack epidemic. Rather, the report concluded that “influential politicians, social activists, and journalists played a central role in propagating the myth of a crack epidemic“. This all begs the question of what role, if any, the CIA actually played in fueling the crack epidemic. After all, the agency did play a pivotal role in escalating the global war on drugs in the 1980s, and crack could easily be described as a “street drug”. It’s important to point out that there’s little question that the drug trade exacerbated the crack epidemic in the 1980s. What is uncertain is whether the CIA actually had any direct role in causing the epidemic, as opposed to simply failing to act when influential people it was involved with were bringing crack to the poorest neighborhoods in America.

How to Stop a Cat from Scratching the Couch
Scratching is a normal and healthy feline behavior, but it can be frustrating when your favorite chair or the arms of your couch become a target. Fortunately, you can train your cat to stop scratching the furniture and other unwanted places.

Understand why cats scratch.
Cats have a natural instinct to scratch. This behavior helps them to remove the dead outer layer of their claws, to keep their claws sharp and healthy, and to mark their territory. 

Provide alternative scratching surfaces.
If you want to stop your cat from scratching the couch, you should provide alternative options. This will allow your cat to continue the behavior in a more appropriate place. The best thing to do is buy a scratching post or pad and place it near the couch. Your cat will probably be more interested in the new scratching post if you place it in the same spot where it used to scratch the couch.

Encourage your cat to use the scratching post.
When you see that your cat is using the scratching post, reward this behavior with lots of affection or a treat. This will help to reinforce the behavior you want to see in your cat.

Use deterrents to stop unwanted scratching.
When you see that your cat is about to scratch the couch, try to stop it by using a deterrent. You can use a noise deterrent, such as a cat scare, to make a loud noise that will startle the cat and prevent it from scratching. You can also use a taste deterrent, such as bitter apple, to make the couch taste unpleasant to the cat.

Be consistent with the training.
To stop a cat from scratching the couch, you will need to be consistent with the training. This means using the deterrent every time you see the cat scratching the couch, and rewarding the cat when it uses the scratching post. With consistent training, your cat will eventually learn that scratching the couch is no longer acceptable.

In this study, we assess the role of planetesimal accretion in the formation of gaseous protoplanets. We outline a sequence of events wherein the transition from small planetary cores to fully-fledged protoplanets can be modulated by residual planetesimals. Evaluation of the mean motion resonances shows that planetesimals cannot pass through these structures, thereby allowing gas to be accreted with little disruption. However, as the protoplanet grows, the resonances overlap, creating an environment for planetesimals to become dynamically unstable. The ensuing gas drag resulting from this instability triggers the migration of planetesimals, which in turn produces a massive bombardment of the protoplanet's surface. Through this mechanism, we explain the discrepant core-envelope structures found in Jupiter and Saturn, as well as the metallic abnormality of many known transiting exoplanets.

Li and Rb are two alkali metal isotopes that exhibit a multitude of temperatures when exposed to thermal radiation from a reservoir. The two isotopes, when isolated from the reservoir of radiation, reach an effective quantum ground state corresponding to a zero-temperature collective state. We demonstrate thermalization of both isotopes to their effective ground state at finite temperature, via a combination of photon scattering and magnetic field control of population and internal state. We also extend the method to atoms with multiple ground states, in this case $^7$Li and $^{87}$Rb, achieving efficient coupling to a single phonon mode in each case. Our results represent a landmark in sympathetic cooling of atoms to temperatures far below the typical modes of a reservoir, and a path to reaching the quantum ground state of multiple species of atoms via a combination of laser cooling and magnetic control. Our two-photon Raman scheme allows for efficient, on-demand coupling of Li and Rb atoms to the deep optical molasses (Doppler) state atoms. First, we address cooling to the ground state by coupling to a single phonon mode, the scissors mode, using a pair of Raman lasers tuned to the $2\,^2S_{1/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2P_{3/2}$ and $2\,^2P_{1/2} \rightarrow 2\,^2S_{1/2}$ transitions. The scissors mode is a collective motion of Li and Rb atoms with zero point energy equal to $k_B\times$288nK, where nK is the temperature in units of 0.1K. We characterize the temperature of the scissors mode by coupling to this mode and measuring the change in momentum distribution of the atoms, finding the mode temperature to be $288\pm29$nK. We then achieve quantum ground state temperatures of Li and Rb by transferring population to the quantum ground state using three Raman lasers and an adiabatic rapid passage (ARap) technique. We measure the final state purity, which approaches unity, as well as the entropy of the system, which we calculate to be equivalent to the zero-point energy of the scissors mode. Finally, we cool $^{87}$Rb to the zero-point energy of the scissors mode by repeating the process starting from the ground state. We find a total entropy reduction of $21.4\pm0.8$nK in three cooling stages. We use a reservoir of radiation to set the atoms’ temperature. We demonstrate that Li and Rb reach their effective quantum ground state at finite temperature through scattering of thermal radiation. We isolate Li in the $2\,^2S_{1/2}$ ground state and Rb in $2\,^2P_{1/2}$ and $2\,^2P_{3/2}$ ground states, and couple the atoms to the vacuum of a cavity via a dipole coupling to a mechanically compliant rod near the cavity

4. While the tools are sanitizing, add 2 quarts of the bottled water to the saucepan and bring to a boil.

5. Use some of your Clorox® to sanitize the work area. This is important to do so that you don't contaminate the beer.

6. After 30 minutes remove all the tools. Make sure to discard the Clorox®/water solution once you are done.

7. Add 1 Cup Sugar to the boiling water in the saucepan. This will provide the necessary food source for the yeast.

8. Add the ice and one gallon of the bottled water to the fermenting bucket. Stir until the mixture begins to cool to room temperature.

9. Pour in the sugar water mix from the saucepan. This will add the necessary sugar for the yeast to start fermenting.

10. Use the remaining bottled water to bring the water level up to approximately 11 Quarts.

11. Place the fermenter in a cool, dark place for 7-14 days. During that time the beer will be fermenting and creating carbon dioxide.

12. After Fermenting, Put 1 teaspoon of Clorox® in 1 gallon (3.8 L) of water. This solution will be used to sanitize each bottle before bottling the beer.

Despite the seemingly minor impact of a plague of frogs, their significance in ancient Egyptian culture cannot be understated. Frogs were seen as symbols of fertility, abundance, and prosperity in Egyptian mythology. They were also associated with the goddess Heket, who was believed to have created the first frogs out of the mud of the Nile. As such, frogs were considered sacred and protected animals in Egyptian society.

The use of battletoads, or frogs, in the plagues inflicted upon Egypt was therefore highly symbolic and deeply meaningful. It was a direct attack on the Egyptian gods and their power. By unleashing plagues of frogs, God was demonstrating his superiority over the gods of Egypt, who were believed to have control over the natural world.

Furthermore, the plagues of frogs had very real agricultural implications. The sudden influx of frogs would have disrupted the delicate balance of the ecosystem and damaged the crops that the Egyptians relied upon for sustenance. The Nile River, which was central to their way of life, would have been overrun with the creatures, making it nearly impossible to use for irrigation and transportation.

In this way, the plagues of frogs were a devastating blow to the very heart of Egyptian society. They were a symbol of God's power and authority, and a demonstration of his ability to control the natural world. While they may seem like a minor inconvenience compared to other plagues, their impact on ancient Egypt cannot be ignored.

An autonomous distributed admission control scheme for IEEE 802.11 DCF is proposed, which can intelligently allocate the channel capacity for improving the utilization efficiency of the wireless medium and fully utilizing the capacity of the available bandwidth. The admission control scheme consists of a controlling mechanism and a controlled algorithm. The controlling mechanism divides the overall network into a number of virtual channels with a fixed size through assigning a range of channel access priorities. All stations in the network sense the wireless medium and calculate the corresponding transmission data rates. The controlled algorithm selects the stations for establishing connections in the controlling mechanism according to their network requirements and moves the whole network among different virtual channels according to the scheduling results. Simulation results show that the channel utilization efficiency can be enhanced effectively. How to Make a Motorcycle Diaper Cake
Making someone a motorcycle diaper cake is an easy and fun way to surprise a new or expectant mother. It's a creative and innovative way to give a birthday gift or baby shower gift that's sure to be appreciated. Not only is it a wonderful gift, but it will give the expectant mom something to decorate her nursery with. Follow the tips below to create a motorcycle diaper cake that's sure to be a hit!

Purchasing the Requirements
The first step to making a motorcycle diaper cake is to purchase the items needed for the cake. Depending on your budget, you may opt to buy all the items in one store or shop around for the best deals. A list of required items includes: 
• diapers 
• decorative ribbon 
• two receiving blankets 
• one baby bib 
• one stuffed toy 
• one baby bottle 
• one ring toy 
• two baby socks 
• tissue paper 

Assembling the Cake
Once you have all the required items for assembling the motorcycle diaper cake, it's time to start the process. Begin by lining the cake pan with several folded diapers. You'll want to layer the diapers until you have about two inches on the sides of the pan. Secure the diapers in place so they don't fall out when you remove the cake from the pan.

Next, remove the cake from the pan and carefully place it on a hard surface. Place the second diaper tire inside the first diaper tire and then wrap both tires with almost all of the decorative ribbon. Leave the end of the ribbon uncut so that you can secure the diaper "tires" together.

Next, begin assembling the handlebars for the motorcycle. To do this, fold one of the receiving blankets in half length-wise and roll it into a very tight roll. Then slide the roll through the diaper tire hole. Stand the diaper tire on its side (so that it looks like a tire) and then fold the second blanket in half length-wise. Place the blanket into the opening of the front tire and then pin the bib (motorcycle's seat) to the top of the front diaper tire.

To finish the handlebars, hold the ends of the front diaper tire blanket upward and then insert the baby bottle (the motorcycle's dashboard) above the bib and underneath the ring toy (the motorcycle's mirror). Create more definition and strength in the handlebars by stuffing the baby socks with a small amount of tissue paper to puff up the garment. Once this is done, top the handlebars with one sock on each side. 

The Final Touches
The last step is to add the decorations to the motorcycle diaper cake. Add the second bib to the back diaper tire the same way you added the first bib to the front. Then, prop the stuffed toy on top so it appears that the toy is riding the motorcycle. Finally, add additional decorative ribbon to the bottom of the diaper to give the cake a more finished appearance.

Congratulations! You have now created a unique, creative and memorable motorcycle diaper cake that the expectant mom is sure to love. Anyone can make a motorcycle diaper cake - just a little bit of creativity, some of the required items, and a few simple steps and you have a finished product that is sure to be appreciated.

The far east was very familiar with Greek culture through direct trade, and the famous philosopher Plato was a pupil of Socrates, who was famously active in China. Chinese writings also frequently reference concepts from Greek philosophy. The inclusion of Greek geometry into the original epigraphical formula of the great wall is another example of this transmission of knowledge. As for the Romans, chinese visitors to Rome in this period were extremely surprised by just how sophisticated Rome's civilization seemed to them. While they were very familiar with the Greeks, the Romans stood out as a much more novel idea. The Chinese wrote down an extremely detailed description of a visit to Rome in one period book, complete with detailed descriptions of buildings, sculpture and military equipment. While the far east was familiar with the Iron Age kingdoms of Europe, the Roman influence would really only become fully understood much later, after the fall of the Roman empire.

This article presents a hydrodynamical algorithm as a tool to study astrophysical detonations, with a specific aim of simulating the carbon detonation that occurs in a superburst event. The algorithm is based on the MUSCL scheme of van Leer and is second-order accurate. Tests performed using the algorithm demonstrate it to be reliable. Preliminary one-dimensional studies show that the carbon detonation process is a multi-scale phenomenon, with the liberation of energy occurring on a length scale $10^6$ times smaller than the total reaction length. It is suggested that a multi-resolution approach can be used to tackle all the reaction lengths. Thermodynamic and composition profiles for different layers of carbon, iron and helium relevant to superbursts are also provided.

Survivor (franchise) is the world's largest reality competition franchise. It was created in 2000 by producer Charlie Parsons and was developed by Mark Burnett for the American television network CBS. The premise of the series involves contestants, known as Survivors, competing in challenges and strategizing to outwit each other in order to be the last one standing and become the Sole Survivor. The show has spawned 35 versions in more than 40 countries around the globe, making it one of the most successful franchises in television history, with over 500 million viewers worldwide. The original version of Survivor, Survivor: Borneo, saw 16 castaways attempt to outlast each other in physical and mental challenges, and strategically form alliances, for 39 days. After being marooned on the remote tropical location, the castaways were forced to survive on their wits with few food and supplies beyond a few simple tools. The series was met with high ratings, which eventually spawned numerous international versions, spin-offs, and board games. Since debuting in 2000, the series has seen countless evolutions, most notably introducing twists to the basic format, such as Redemption Island, Exile Island and hidden immunity idols. Additionally, each version offers its own culturally-specific civilization building challenges and rewards, allowing each show to tailor to its individual audience. The franchise has also won multiple awards, including an Emmy Award, four Critics' Choice Awards, an International Emmy Award and a Golden Globe. It has also been credited with helping to launch the career of several former contestants, including Sandra Diaz-Twine, who became the only two-time champion on the United States version of the show; Yul Kwon, who competed on the thirteenth season and later becoming the host of ABC’s Primetime: What Would You Do; and Richard Hatch, the original winner of Survivor: Borneo. In addition to the television series, the Survivor franchise encompasses a wide range of merchandise, from board games and shirt to DVDs, books and even video games. With its iconic "Outwit, Outplay, Outlast" tagline and its impact on modern television, Survivor has become a worldwide sensation and has established itself as one of the most successful and enduring franchises of all time.

In this work, we present a systematic scan for 7-colourings of the grid, aiming to find all possible ways to colour a rectangular grid of size m×n using seven distinct colours. We use a divide-and-conquer approach, where we decompose the grid into smaller sub-grids and find all possible 7-colourings for each sub-grid, and then combine them to form a 7-colouring for the entire grid.

The motivation for this research lies in the need to understand the colouring properties of grids, which have applications in various fields such as graph theory, computer vision, and telecommunications. By presenting an exhaustive list of 7-colourings of the grid, we contribute to the development of methods for optimising grid colourings in these fields.

Our results show that the number of 7-colourings of the grid increases rapidly as the size of the grid increases. For example, we found 8,065,328 distinct 7-colourings for a 4x4 grid, while for a 5x5 grid, we found 630,880,211 distinct 7-colourings. Furthermore, we observed that there exist symmetrical 7-colourings that are invariant under certain reflections, rotations, or translations.

In conclusion, our systematic scan for 7-colourings of the grid provides a comprehensive list of all possible ways to colour rectangular grids using seven colours and offers insights into the colouring properties of grids.
