We present a new algorithm for computing the magnetic field in a protoplanetary disk based on the magnetohydrodynamic equations. Our method does not require the introduction of any empirical model, such as the magnetic field amplification factor. We obtain a good agreement with the observations of the magnetic field in the solar nebula, as well as in the disks around other stars. The new algorithm is based on an adequate spatial sampling and the proper treatment of the divergence of the magnetic field, taking into account the azimuthal and radial variations of the field in the disk. In addition, we propose a new parameterization of the magnetic field in the disk, which allows a simple evaluation of the field in the plane of the disk. Our results show that the magnetic field is generated mainly in the upper part of the disk, with a minimum value in the midplane, in agreement with the observations. We also show that the field in the plane is mainly toroidal, with a contribution of about one order of magnitude higher than the poloidal component, in agreement with the predictions of the Parker instability theory. Finally, we discuss the problem of the formation of the magnetic field in the disk, and we analyze the physical properties of the magnetic grains that might be responsible for the generation of the field.

We consider the Lieb-Oxford bound on the energies of entangled states of massive particles. We show that this bound is tight for all possible entangled states of massive particles and therefore rules out a number of potential extensions of quantum mechanics that would relax this bound. This rules out, in particular, any version of hidden variables theory in which the bound is relaxed, unless the physical parameters of the theory are such that massive particles can be prepared in states that do not correspond to a well-defined position-momentum pair. We show that such states can be achieved in a version of hidden variables theory in which the position and momentum operators do not commute, provided that the bound is replaced by a weaker one that still holds for all states of massive particles. We show further that this still rules out a number of hidden variables theories that are usually considered to be candidates for a theory beyond quantum mechanics. We then consider a generalization of the Lieb-Oxford bound to a class of noncommutative probability spaces that includes as a special case the probability spaces of quantum mechanics. We show that this generalization of the bound is equivalent to the original one, in that it rules out any extension of quantum mechanics in which the bound is relaxed.

These measurements are made over a range of transverse separations corresponding to physical scales ranging from 2 h-1 Mpc to 20 h-1 Mpc. In addition, we also measure the real-space two-point correlation function by applying the method developed by Eisenstein et al. (2007) . This measurement is performed only out to a maximum separation of 60 h-1 Mpc due to the limited number density of our galaxy sample.

He also taught music at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music and Sonoma State University. Sender was a major influence on the development of electronic music, and his contributions helped pave the way for future generations of electronic musicians. He passed away on February 14, 2019, in San Francisco.

Auxvasse Creek is a 71.8-mile-long creek in north-central Missouri in the United States. It runsthrough Audrain, Monroe and Montgomery counties. The source of the Auxvasse Creek is located in southeastern Audrain County, located in the north-central portion of Missouri. It then runs north-northwest passing through Montgomery County and then turning northwest following US Highway 54 passing by the community of Auxvasse in western Callaway County. In Lewistown the creek turns more northerly and passes Colesburg and eventually enters the Salt River northwest of Clark in northeast Montgomery County. The Main Fork of Auxvasse Creek passes through Audrain, Monroe and Montgomery counties and is a tributary of the Salt River near Clark. In total, three major branches of the Auxvasse Creek network supply watershed areas in north-central Missouri. The Auxvasse Creek watershed provides a natural platform for supporting many recreational activities which include fishing, hunting, canoeing, kayaking, swimming, camping and nature study. The area is also rich with bird life, playgrounds, and other outdoor recreational opportunities. The Auxvasse Creek area is an excellent location for a variety of forms of outdoor exploration and discovery year-round. Auxvasse Creek is the headwaters of many of the tributary streams, including Buttermilk Creek, Wolf Creek, Sinking Creek, and Commerce Creek. Buttermilk Creek, a tributary of Auxvasse Creek, is a 28-mile-long stream that connects with Wolf and Sinking Creeks in northern Montgomery County. Wolf Creek is a 9.3-mile-long stream that also runs through the Auxvasse Watershed. Other notable tributaries of Auxvasse Creek are McCoy Creek, Brush Creek, and Indian Creek. The Auxvasse Creek is the host of several fishing tournaments conducted annually in the area. Many different species of fish inhabit the creek, including catfish, bass, sunfish, carp and channel catfish, as well as other species. The Auxvasse Creek Watershed is home to many different species of plants and animals, offering a rich ecosystem vital to the health of its inhabitants and the surrounding areas. From a geological point of view, the Auxvasse Creek is a part of the northern Mississippi River Valley. Auxvasse Creek is part of the floodplain which, combined with the various tributaries, supplies the area with a natural resource for recreational activities as well as providing important ground for supporting ecosystems. In August 1984, Auxvasse Creek was declared a State Inland Waterway by the Missouri Department of Natural Resources. This designation places Auxvasse Creek in a special category that allows certain industrial and water development activities to occur in the watershed under rigid guidelines and regulations. This provides an investment opportunity that increases the importance and value of this unique creek. The Auxvasse Creek and its tributaries are essential water resources in central Missouri. These watersheds provide an avenue for recreation, protect the environment, and offer businesses an opportunity to invest in the area. The Auxvasse Creek watershed is a valuable subject of study and consideration and should be protected, preserved and enjoyed.

Parasites have been a constant human companion since prehistoric times and the Vikings were no exception. In fact, the Vikings likely faced an even greater risk of parasitic infection than most other ancient civilizations due to their lifestyle, which often involved unsanitary living conditions and close contact with animals.

So how did people deal with parasites in the olden days? The answer varies depending on the time period and geographical location, but there are a few common remedies that have been used throughout history. One of the most popular remedies was the use of herbs and plants, many of which are still used today to treat parasitic infections. For example, garlic and onion were often consumed in large quantities as they were believed to be effective against parasites. Other plants such as wormwood, black walnut, and clove were also commonly used to treat intestinal worms.

In addition to herbal remedies, people in the olden days would often try to prevent parasitic infections by practicing good hygiene. This meant regularly washing hands, clothes, and bedding, as well as avoiding contact with contaminated water and soil. In some cases, people would even use hygiene-related methods such as enemas or bloodletting to rid themselves of parasites.

Of course, not all methods of dealing with parasites were effective. Many old-time remedies were based on superstition rather than science, and some were downright dangerous. For example, in medieval times it was common to use mercury, which is highly toxic, to treat parasitic infections.

In the end, dealing with parasites in the olden days was a mixed bag. While some remedies were effective, many were not, and people often had to suffer through parasitic infections without any relief. Fortunately, modern medicine has come a long way since then, and we now have a variety of safe and effective treatments for parasitic infections.

Write a long abstract of a scientific paper from arXiv.org. Use approximately 200-400 words.
Title: "The formation of S0 galaxies: evidence from globular clusters".
Abstract:
We present new results on the properties and evolution of early-type galaxies (ETGs) in the Coma cluster, based on deep HST/ACS imaging data obtained as part of our ongoing survey for faint globular clusters associated with ETGs.  We find that the majority of brightest cluster members are elliptical or lenticular galaxies, while only one galaxy is classified as an S0/a galaxy. The fraction of S0s increases towards fainter luminosities, reaching about 50% at M V = −18 mag. This result suggests that most S0s were formed through morphological transformation of late-type spirals during their infall into the cluster environment. In addition to this morphological transformation scenario, we also consider other possible mechanisms such as ram pressure stripping by intracluster gas and tidal interactions between galaxies. By comparing the observed number density profiles of globular clusters around different types of ETGs, we show that there exists no significant difference among these three populations.

LSD (Lysergic Acid Diethylamide) is a powerful hallucinogenic drug that alters the user’s perception, thinking, and emotion. It is naturally derived from ergot, a fungus that grows on rye and other grains and is also produced in a laboratory environment.

Upon ingestion, LSD is quickly absorbed into and circulates throughout the bloodstream. It then enters into the central nervous system, where it binds to serotonin receptors in the brain. This connection changes the way users view the world around them because serotonin is a neurotransmitter responsible for regulating numerous aspects of behavior and cognition, including mood, anxiety, and perception.

Effects can be felt as early as 30 minutes after ingestion, and peaks at 1-2 hours after, depending on the dose taken. There is a surge in creativity, time distortion, and uplifting mood as a result of the chemical reaction between the drug and the brain.

Additionally, LSD has been studied for its potential therapeutic benefits. While individuals can experience visual and auditory hallucinations, they often report feeling clear-minded and highly functional while under the influence. During this period of heightened clarity and awareness, users are often able to make connection with their own thought patterns and behaviors.

At higher doses, users might experience more dramatic effects such as synesthesia (senses blending together), depersonalization, and “lowered” cognitive functioning. These dissociative-like effects are more strongly associated with a “bad trip” and can lead to anxiety, confusion, and paranoia.

The effects of an LSD experience are temporary, usually lasting 8 -10 hours. As users come down from the trip, they often report feeling relaxed, introspective, and content. The intensity of the experience can vary greatly from person to person, and is greatly influenced by the user’s mindset and environment when taking the drug. 

All in all, LSD can have both positive and negative effects on the user. Common side effects include elevated heart rate, increased body temperature, dry mouth, nausea, and increased blood pressure. As with any drug, it is important for individuals to be mindful of their safety and to use it responsibly.

Write a long abstract of a scientific paper from arXiv.org. Use approximately 200-400 words.
Title: "Dark Matter in Gauge Mediation from Emergent Supersymmetry".
Abstract:
We propose that the dark matter (DM) and supersymmetric particles are generated by an emergent gauge symmetry at high energy scales, which is broken down to Standard Model symmetries below TeV scale. The DM candidate can be identified as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson associated with spontaneous breaking of global U(1) symmetry. We show how this scenario can explain various experimental results on DM searches including recent LHC data. In addition we discuss possible collider signatures for future experiments such as ILC or CLIC. Introduction: Dark matter (DM), whose existence has been inferred through its gravitational effects over many decades [1] , remains one of the most mysterious phenomena in particle physics today [2] . Although there have been numerous proposals for explaining the origin of DM [3] , none of them has yet provided compelling evidence for their viability [4] .
In this work, motivated by the idea of "emergent" theories [5] - [8] , we consider a new possibility where DM emerges from a spontaneously-broken global symmetry [9] . This approach provides a simple explanation for why DM should exist without introducing any additional fields beyond those already present within the Standard Model [10] . Furthermore, it allows us to identify the DM candidate as a pseudo-NambuGoldstone boson [11] , thereby providing a natural solution to the so-called "WIMP miracle" [12] problem [13] . Finally, our model also predicts the presence of light scalar superpartners [14] , which may provide interesting signals at upcoming high-energy accelerator facilities [15] .
The rest of this article is organised as follows. In Sec. 2, we introduce our theoretical framework based upon emergent gauge mediation [16] . Then, in Secs. 3-7, we demonstrate how this framework can simultaneously address all current experimental constraints [17] - [20] while predicting novel phenomenological features [21] . Finally, in Sec. 8, we conclude with some remarks about further directions of research.

Writing a book can seem like a daunting task, but with the right preparation, it can be an enjoyable and fulfilling experience. Here are some steps to prepare for writing a book:

1. Choose your writing materials. There's no right or wrong way to write, so pick the tools that work best for you. This could include a computer, notebook, typewriter, or even pen and paper.

2. Create an organizational system. Before starting to write, organize your research, notes, and ideas in a way that makes sense to you. This could be through digital folders, index cards, or a physical filing system.

3. Have a regular writing spot. Find a place where you can consistently go to write. This could be a home office, coffee shop, or library. Make sure it's a place where you feel comfortable and can focus.

4. Look for an inspirational writing location. Inspiration strikes every writer differently. Find a location that helps get your creative juices flowing, whether it's a park, beach, or museum.

5. Make your writing space comfortable. Consider adding elements that make your writing spot cozy and inviting, such as a comfortable chair, plants, or artwork.

6. Decorate your writing space. The more you can personalize your writing space, the more time you'll want to spend there. Add decorations that inspire you and reflect your personality.

7. Figure out when you work best. Are you a morning person or a night owl? Determine what times of day you're most productive and try to schedule your writing time accordingly.

8. Consider your other obligations. Make sure to factor in other responsibilities such as work, family, and social commitments. Create a writing schedule that works with your other obligations.

9. Create a writing schedule. A daily writing routine will make you more likely to stick to your goals and finish your book. You should know when you're going to write every day and plan the rest of your schedule around it. Depending on how flexible your day-to-day life is, create either a strict or flexible writing schedule.

10. Make a promise that you won't get drawn away from the routine. Hold yourself accountable for sticking to the schedule and make it a priority.

11. Set deadlines for yourself. Setting deadlines is a delicate balance. Make them realistic and attainable, but also challenging enough to push you to finish your book.

12. Get an accountability partner. An accountability partner is another writer who's also working on a book. You can check in with each other and provide support and motivation.

13. Determine the book's genre. When deciding what type of book you want to write, first consider what types of books you like to read. Choose a genre that excites you and that you feel passionate about.

14. Figure out the book's purpose. Once you've chosen your book's genre, you need to figure out what you want to provide the reader. Are you trying to entertain them, educate them, or inspire them?

15. Conduct your research. If you are writing to provide information, it may seem obvious that you need to spend a lot of time researching. Make sure to conduct thorough research to ensure that your book is accurate and informative.

16. Outline your book. As you research, your vision for the book may start coming together. Create an outline that captures the main themes, ideas, and structure of your book. This will help guide your writing and keep you on track. 

By following these steps and preparing for the writing process, you'll set yourself up for success in writing a book that you can be proud of.

Real medieval cities did have guards, though not exactly as portrayed in video games and fantasy fiction. During medieval times, cities had walls around them and guards to control who entered and left. These city walls were not always made of stone, and sometimes were made of wood. The guards would usually stand in towers and watch over the walls.

In some cities, the guards were armed with spears, swords, clubs, or other weapons. Sometimes they wore armor, while other times they wore only simple clothing. Depending on the city, the guards might keep watch all of the time, or be assigned specific times each day.

In addition to city walls and guards, most cities in medieval times also had walls surrounding their gates. These gates were typically guarded around the clock by one or more full-time guards to keep unwanted visitors and trespassers out. Cities also often had city gates that could be locked overnight or during times of trouble.

Overall, medieval cities did have guards, though the guards didn't look the same or do the same types of things that you might see in video games or fantasy fiction. The guards were responsible for keeping people and things out of the city, rather than adventures and such.

During the Medieval period, identifying which side a soldier was on was a crucial task in the battlefield, given the chaotic nature of warfare. Several methods were employed by Medieval armies to distinguish between their own soldiers and the enemies, including the use of uniforms, flags, banners, insignias, and symbols. Additionally, soldiers might wear identifying marks or accessories, such as badges, colors, or crests, indicating their allegiance to a particular lord, commander, or army. Sometimes, soldiers would shout slogans or battle cries to show their loyalty or challenge the enemy.

However, these identifying methods were not always successful, and soldiers could still be misidentified, especially in the fog of war, or when the opposing army employed similar tactics or clothing. The risk of friendly fire and mistaken identity was evident in many battles throughout the Medieval period. For instance, during the Battle of Agincourt, on October 25, 1415, English soldiers slaughtered several French prisoners who were dressed like the English, leading to a notorious act of violence and confusion.

The likelihood of friendly fire also depended on factors such as the size of the army, the complexity of battle formations, and the level of discipline and training of the soldiers. In smaller armies, soldiers might know each other personally, reducing the chances of misidentifications. In contrast, in larger armies, soldiers might be less familiar with their comrades, leading to higher risks of confusion.

Overall, while Medieval armies employed various methods to distinguish friend from foe, the risk of friendly fire and mistaken identity remained high, leading to casualties and confusion in many battles. Despite the limitations of these methods, soldiers were trained to focus on their objectives and follow commands, even in the heat of battle, to minimize the risks of misidentifications and maximize their chances of victory.

When it comes to cleaning effectiveness, there is a clear difference between a regular manual toothbrush and an electric one. Research has shown that electric toothbrushes are more effective at removing plaque, which is a sticky film of bacteria that builds up on teeth. Plaque is a major cause of tooth decay and gum disease, so using an electric toothbrush can help to reduce the risk of these problems.

Electric toothbrushes also tend to be more effective at cleaning the hard-to-reach areas of the mouth, such as the back teeth and the gum line. This is because they have a rotating or oscillating head that helps to loosen plaque and debris from the teeth.

However, it is important to note that not all electric toothbrushes are created equal. Some models are better than others at removing plaque, and some may be too aggressive for certain people, such as those with sensitive teeth or gum recession.

It is also important to remember that brushing technique and frequency are still important factors in maintaining good oral hygiene. No matter what type of toothbrush you use, it is important to brush your teeth for two minutes twice a day, using a soft-bristled brush and fluoride toothpaste.

We consider a simple model of bacterial growth in which the local population density depends linearly on the local nutrient concentration, and the nutrient diffusion is described by the Keller-Segel equation. We find that the population density has a critical value, below which the population dies out, and above which the population continues to grow. This critical density has a simple expression in terms of the coefficients of the Keller-Segel equation. We show that this critical density has an analogy in the theory of white dwarf stars. In particular, the limiting mass of a white dwarf, below which the star collapses to a neutron star or a black hole, has the same form as the critical density of the bacterial population. We also consider a more general model in which the local population density depends on the local nutrient concentration in a more complicated way. In this case, the critical density has a more involved form, but still has an analogy with the limiting mass of white dwarf stars.

Title: "Near-infrared polarimetric study of the bipolar nebula IRAS 19312+1950".
Abstract:
We present near-infrared (NIR) polarimetry and spectroscopy for the bipolar reflection nebula IRAS 19312; 1950 . The NIR polarization vectors are aligned with those in optical images, indicating that they trace scattered light from an illuminating source located behind the dense molecular cloud core. We find evidence for two distinct scattering regions along our line-of-sight to this object; one is associated with the brightest part of the nebula, while another region shows lower polarization degrees but higher polarized fluxes at longer wavelengths. These results suggest that there may be multiple sources contributing to the observed emission. In addition, we detect several absorption features which can be attributed to water ice on dust grains near the central star(s). Our observations also reveal a possible outflow cavity traced by blueshifted CO emission lines. Cosmic rays interact with gas to produce a range of chemical products. In this work we show that this process also modifies the elemental composition of the gas. We apply our model to the gas observed in the prsent day universe and show that, although the Xelement enhancement is typically much lower than in high-z systems, it is able to reproduce the general trend. Finally we show that the evolution of the enhancement depends strongly on the shape of the cosmic ray spectrum at low energy. We apply our model to a broad range of spectra and show that different spectra lead to Xelement enhancements at the level of $10^{-3} - 1$ solar values at $z = 0$ for different metallicities at $10^{-4}$ solar values. This wide range of possible enhancements highlights the importance of experimental studies of the early evolution of the Universe. We describe an effect whereby the interactions between cosmic rays and the primordial gas influence both the gas phase and the element abundances. This has important implications for the potentiality of the gas to form structures and for the evolution of the heavy element abundance with time. We apply our model to the gas observed in the present-day Universe and show that although the general trend of the Xelement enhancement is lower than in high-redshift systems, it is still sufficient to reproduce the general trend. We also show that the evolution of the enhancement strongly depends on the shape of the cosmic ray spectrum at low energy. Our work highlights the importance of experimental studies of the early evolution of the Universe and the need to obtain a better understanding of processes occurring at low energies, such as the interaction between cosmic rays and the gas in the early universe. We provide a formalism for computing the evolution of the chemical abundances, including the element abundance enhancement, starting from a given ionisation and chemical networks and a given spectrum of cosmic rays. The results of the calculations are self-consistent as they can be fed back into the ionisation and chemical networks. The new networks have to be specified in terms of the twelve essential reactions needed to generate the sixteen molecules containing a significant fraction of the enhanced elements and a full network for eleven further elements (B, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, K, Ca, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ni, Cu, Zn, Sr, Y, Zr, Nb, Mo, Ta, W, Re, Ru, Os, Hg, Tl, Pb, Bi, and Po). The updated chemical composition can strongly impact the cooling/heating rates of the gas, the star formation, and the gravitational collapse and further enrichment of the gas. The effects described in this work are not restricted to the epoch of reionization but extend to any time in the history of the gas, until the gas is removed from the simulation by some feedback mechanism. Insulin-degrading enzyme (IDE) is a zinc metalloprotease shown to be responsible for the progression of many types of cancer through the degradation of insulin, insulin-like growth factors and other growth factors. In the current study, several human tissue types were evaluated for the expression of IDE, and many previously reported findings were confirmed. The strongest IDE staining was seen in breast, prostate, liver and pancreas tissue. Surprisingly, some previously reported IDE-positive normal human tissue types (including: brain, eye, kidney and small intestine) were demonstrated to be negative for IDE, and in a few instances, the opposite was true (i.e. some IDE-negative normal human tissue types were shown to be positive for IDE). These findings raise doubts about the validity of many previous studies examining the expression of IDE in normal and neoplastic human tissue. *Citation: Jaggo N, Jalkanmaa M, Mannisto P, Saloheimo J (2018) Immunohistochemical pitfalls in the demonstration of insulin-degrading enzyme in normal and neoplastic human tissues.
